summary.text: For \(n=67\), the distinct values \(m=147,2055,32773\) all satisfy \(\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor\log_2 m\rfloor}(m\bmod 2^k)=67\) (their residue sums are respectively \(1+3+3+3+19+19+19\), \(1+3+9\cdot7\), and \(1+1+13\cdot5\)). Thus at least three values are counted at \(67\), contradicting the claimed count of one.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor\log_2 m\rfloor}\bigl(m\bmod 2^k\bigr)
\]
be the value of A049802 at the index \(m\). For \(n>0\), the definition of A383327 used in the conjecture is
\[
a(n)=\#\{m:0\le m<2^{n+1}\text{ and }T(m)=n\}.
\]
(The range \(m<2^{n+1}\) is a sufficient finite range for counting all occurrences.) We will disprove the conjecture at the listed value \(n=67\) by exhibiting three distinct indices in this range at which A049802 has value \(67\).

First take \(m=147\). Since
\[
2^7=128\le 147<256=2^8,
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 147\rfloor=7\). The required remainders are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccc}
k&1&2&3&4&5&6&7\\ \hline
147\bmod 2^k&1&3&3&3&19&19&19.
\end{array}
\]
Indeed, \(147=128+19\); reducing further gives remainder \(3\) modulo \(16\), \(8\), and \(4\), and remainder \(1\) modulo \(2\). Consequently
\[
T(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67.
\]

Next take \(m=2055=2^{11}+7\). Because
\[
2^{11}\le2055<2^{12},
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 2055\rfloor=11\). For every \(k\) with \(3\le k\le11\), the number \(2^k\) divides \(2^{11}\), while \(0\le7<2^k\). Hence
\[
2055\bmod 2^k=7\qquad(3\le k\le11).
\]
For the two smaller powers, the remainders are
\[
2055\bmod2=1,\qquad 2055\bmod4=3.
\]
There are nine integers \(k\) from \(3\) through \(11\), so
\[
T(2055)=1+3+9\cdot7=67.
\]

Finally take \(m=32773=2^{15}+5\). We have
\[
2^{15}\le32773<2^{16},
\]
so \(\lfloor\log_2 32773\rfloor=15\). For every \(k\) with \(3\le k\le15\), \(2^k\) divides \(2^{15}\) and \(5<2^k\), and therefore
\[
32773\bmod 2^k=5\qquad(3\le k\le15).
\]
For \(k=1,2\), the remainders are both \(1\), since \(32773\) is congruent to \(5\) modulo \(4\). There are thirteen integers from \(3\) through \(15\), and thus
\[
T(32773)=1+1+13\cdot5=67.
\]

The three indices \(147\), \(2055\), and \(32773\) are pairwise distinct. They also all belong to the range used to define \(a(67)\): indeed,
\[
147<2055<32773<2^{16}<2^{68}=2^{67+1}.
\]
It follows that the set
\[
F=\{m:0\le m<2^{68}\text{ and }T(m)=67\}
\]
contains the three-element subset
\[
\{147,2055,32773\}.
\]
Therefore \(\#F\ge3\). Since \(67\ne0\), the nonzero branch of the definition of \(a\) gives
\[
a(67)=\#F\ge3,
\]
and in particular
\[
a(67)\ne1.
\]

Now let
\[
S=\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}.
\]
The conjecture claims that every \(n\in S\) satisfies \(a(n)=1\). But \(67\in S\), so the conjecture would imply \(a(67)=1\), contradicting the explicit lower bound \(a(67)\ge3\) above. Hence the conjecture is false.
